title: Understanding Kriging (Part 2)
text:
3.1 Gaussian Random Fields
A random field \(Y\) on \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) is called a Gaussian Random Field (GRF) if, for any finite collection of locations \(\mathbf{s}_1, \dots, \mathbf{s}_n \in D\), the joint distribution of \((Y(\mathbf{s}_1), \dots, Y(\mathbf{s}_n))^\top\) is multivariate Gaussian:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} Y(\mathbf{s}_1) \\ \vdots \\ Y(\mathbf{s}_n) \end{pmatrix}
\sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\mu},\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right),
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (\mu(\mathbf{s}_1), \dots, \mu(\mathbf{s}_n))^\top\) is the mean vector and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is the \(n \times n\) covariance matrix with entries \(\Sigma_{ij} = \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{s}_j)\).
A GRF is therefore entirely characterized by its mean function \(\mu(\mathbf{s})\) and covariance function \(\sigma^2 \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}')\). We write \(Y \sim \mathcal{GRF}(\mu, \sigma^2 \mathbf{C})\) to denote this. This characterization is what makes GRFs so tractable: all finite-dimensional distributions are Gaussian, and conditional distributions — the key operation for prediction — remain Gaussian and can be computed in closed form.

title: Understanding Kriging (Part 2)
text:
3.2 Stationarity
A GRF is called second-order stationary (or weakly stationary) if:

The mean is constant: \(\mu(\mathbf{s}) = \mu\) for all \(\mathbf{s} \in D\).
The covariance depends only on the lag vector \(\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{s} - \mathbf{s}'\):

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(Y(\mathbf{s}),\, Y(\mathbf{s}')) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{s} - \mathbf{s}') = \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{h}).
\]
If the covariance depends only on the Euclidean distance \(r = \|\mathbf{h}\|\) and not on the direction, the field is called isotropic:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(Y(\mathbf{s}),\, Y(\mathbf{s}')) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}(\|\mathbf{s} - \mathbf{s}'\|).
\]
Isotropy reduces the covariance function to a univariate function of distance, which greatly simplifies both modeling and parameter estimation. We assume isotropy throughout.

title: Understanding Kriging (Part 2)
text:
3.4 Kriging as Bayesian Prediction
We now frame spatial prediction within the Bayesian paradigm. Suppose we observe \(\mathbf{y} = (y(\mathbf{s}_1), \dots, y(\mathbf{s}_N))^\top\) and wish to predict the unknown value \(Y(\mathbf{s}_*)\) at a new location \(\mathbf{s}_*\). We adopt the hierarchical model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y(\mathbf{s}) &= \mu + U(\mathbf{s}), \qquad U \sim \mathcal{GRF}(0,\, \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}), \\
y(\mathbf{s}_i) &= Y(\mathbf{s}_i) + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma_e^2),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\mu\) is the constant mean, \(U(\mathbf{s})\) is the zero-mean latent GRF with process variance \(\sigma^2\) and correlation function \(\mathbf{C}\), and \(\varepsilon_i\) is independent Gaussian measurement noise with variance \(\sigma_e^2\) — called the nugget in geostatistics. The nugget accounts for both instrument error and microscale variability that cannot be resolved at the observation scale.
Define the cross-covariance vector \(\mathbf{k}_* = \sigma^2\mathbf{c}_*\), where \(\mathbf{c}_* = (\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_*), \dots, \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{s}_N, \mathbf{s}_*))^\top\) collects the correlations between the observation sites and the prediction site. The joint distribution of observations and prediction target is then:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{y} \\ Y_* \end{pmatrix}
\sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix} \mu \mathbf{1} \\ \mu \end{pmatrix},\;
\begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{y}} & \mathbf{k}_* \\ \mathbf{k}_*^\top & \sigma^2 \end{pmatrix}
\right),
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{y}} = \sigma^2 \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{S}, \mathbf{S}) + \sigma_e^2 \mathbf{I}\) is the \(N \times N\) observation covariance matrix, with \((i,j)\) entry \(\sigma^2\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{s}_j) + \sigma_e^2\mathbf{1}_{[i=j]}\).

3.4.1 The Kriging Equations
By the standard formula for the conditional distribution of a partitioned multivariate Gaussian, the posterior of \(Y_* = Y(\mathbf{s}_*)\) given the data is:
\[
\boxed{Y_* \mid \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\hat{y}_*, \, \sigma^2_*\right),}
\]
with Kriging mean:
\[
\hat{y}_* = \mu + \mathbf{k}_*^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{y}}^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - \mu \mathbf{1}),
\]
and Kriging variance:
\[
\sigma^2_* = \sigma^2 - \mathbf{k}_*^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{y}}^{-1} \mathbf{k}_*,
\]
where \(\mathbf{k}_* = \sigma^2\mathbf{c}_*\) is the cross-covariance vector defined above. Several key properties follow immediately:

Exact interpolation: if \(\sigma_e^2 = 0\) (no nugget), the Kriging mean passes exactly through the observations, i.e. \(\hat{y}_{\mathbf{s}_i} = y(\mathbf{s}_i)\), and the variance \(\sigma^2_*\) collapses to zero at those locations.
Reversion to prior: as \(\mathbf{s}_*\) moves far from all observation sites, \(\mathbf{k}_* \to \mathbf{0}\), so \(\hat{y}_* \to \mu\) and \(\sigma^2_* \to \sigma^2\) — the prediction falls back to the prior mean with full prior uncertainty.
Uncertainty is design-dependent: \(\sigma^2_*\) depends only on the spatial configuration \(\{\mathbf{s}_i\}\) and \(\mathbf{s}_*\), not on the observed values \(\mathbf{y}\). This means the prediction uncertainty can be evaluated — and the survey design can be optimized — before collecting data.



3.4.2 Practical Computation via Cholesky
Direct inversion of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{y}}\) is numerically unstable for large \(N\). In practice we use the Cholesky decomposition \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top\) and define the weight vector:
\[
\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{y}}^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \mu\mathbf{1}),
\]
computed via two triangular solves: forward-solve \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{y} - \mu\mathbf{1}\), then back-solve \(\mathbf{L}^\top\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \mathbf{v}\). The Kriging mean and variance then become:
\[
\hat{y}_* = \mu + \mathbf{k}_*^\top \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \qquad
\sigma^2_* = \sigma^2 - \|\mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{k}_*\|^2,
\]
where \(\|\mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{k}_*\|^2 = \mathbf{v}_*^\top\mathbf{v}_*\) with \(\mathbf{v}_* = \mathbf{L}^{-1}\mathbf{k}_*\) obtained by a forward solve. The Cholesky factorization costs \(\mathcal{O}(N^3)\) and is performed once; each subsequent prediction requires only \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) operations. This is the standard approach in all production Kriging implementations.

title: About me
text:
I am currently a member of the Chair of Optimization and Inverse Problems at Stuttgart Universi"at. My research focuses on solving dynamic inverse problems using Bayesian inference and scientific computing. Prior to this, I was a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Spatial Data Science and Statistical Learning at Georg-August-Universi"at G"ottingen. I also worked one year at the Chair of Geoinformatics–Big Spatial Data at Universi"at Bayreuth.
My doctoral thesis was supervised by Javier Contreras Reyes and Michael Karkulik, where I proposed computational methods to incorporate smoothing thin plate splines into spatial models. During my doctoral studies, I completed two research internships: the first in the Probabilistic Machine Learning group at Aalto University, under the supervision of Aki Vehtari; and the second in the Computer, Electrical, and Mathematical Sciences and Engineering Division at KAUST, under the supervision of Paula Moraga. In addition to my academic experience, I have worked as a Data Scientist in the retail (Cencosud–Scotiabank) and forest (Arauco Celulosa) industries. title: Understanding Kriging (Part 1)
text:
In this first blog post, I would like to share my thoughts on how the Kriging method can often lead to confusion due to its different interpretations. My goal is to help readers distinguish between Kriging (the “Best Linear Unbiased Predictor (BLUP)”) viewed from the linear algebra perspective (as a solution of a linear system of equations) and its probabilistic interpretation as a Gaussian random field (the term “Gaussian process” I prefer using it for data without a spatial reference).
In Part 1, I will present the equations used to calculate the Kriging weights and demonstrate how to predict values at specific spatial locations. Using these weights, we will then perform interpolation over a regular square grid covering the entire spatial domain of interest. Finally, the results from our manual calculations will be compared with those obtained using the “gstat” package to assess their consistency and accuracy.

title: Understanding Kriging (Part 1)
text:
3.1 Empirical Variogram
Traditionally, the selection of a variogram model begins with plotting the empirical semivariogram. This empirical plot is then visually compared against various theoretical models to identify the most appropriate fit. The standard form of the empirical semivariogram is given by
\[
\hat{\gamma}(\mathbf{h}) = \frac{1}{2n(\mathbf{h})} \sum^{n(\mathbf{h})}_{i,j}(Z(\mathbf{s}_i) - Z(\mathbf{s}_j))^{2},
\tag{4}\]
where \(Z(\mathbf{s}_i)\) and \(Z(\mathbf{s}_j)\) are the values (in the space) at the spatial locations \(\mathbf{s}\). Finally, we will denote the variogram as \(2 \gamma(\mathbf{h})\).









The typical variogram models are:

Exponential:
\(\gamma(\mathbf{h}) = \sigma^2 \left(1 - \exp\left(-\frac{\mathbf{h}}{\rho}\right)\right)\)
Spherical:
\[\begin{equation*}
\gamma(\mathbf{h}) =
\begin{cases}
\sigma^2 \left[\frac{3\mathbf{h}}{2\rho} - \frac{\mathbf{h}^3}{2\rho^3}\right], & \text{if } 0 \le \mathbf{h} \le \rho \\\sigma^2, & \text{if } \mathbf{h} > \rho
\end{cases}
\end{equation*}\]
Gaussian:
\(\gamma(\mathbf{h}) = \sigma^2 \left(1 - \exp\left(-\left(\frac{\mathbf{h}}{\rho}\right)^2\right)\right)\)

For all the variograms presented, \(\rho\) is the range parameter.

title: Understanding Kriging (Part 1)
text:
4.1 Practical example


Given the following observed values:
\[\begin{equation*}
Z(\mathbf{s}_1) = 10, \hspace{2mm} Z(\mathbf{s}_2) = 12, \hspace{2mm} Z(\mathbf{s}_3) = 14, \hspace{2mm} Z(\mathbf{s}_4) = 13, \hspace{2mm} Z(\mathbf{s}_5) = 15
\end{equation*}\]
and the corresponding distances between the spatial points (the distance matrix)
\[\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\
2 & 0 & 2 & 4 & 6 \\
4 & 2 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\
6 & 4 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\
8 & 6 & 4 & 2 & 0
\end{bmatrix}\]
Calculate the experimental variogram for the distance \(\mathbf{h} = 2\).
Solution: The empirical variogram estimator \(\hat{\gamma}(\mathbf{h})\) for \(\mathbf{h}\) is defined as:
\[\begin{equation*}
\hat{\gamma}(\mathbf{h}) = \frac{1}{2 n(\mathbf{h})} \sum^{n(\mathbf{h})}_{i,j} \left( Z(\mathbf{s}_i) - Z(\mathbf{s}_j) \right)^2,
\end{equation*}\]
where \(n(\mathbf{h})\) is the number of pairs \((i, j)\) such that the distance between \(\mathbf{s}_i\) and \(\mathbf{s}_j\) is approximately \(\mathbf{h}\).

For \(\mathbf{h} = 2\), the pairs of points whose distance is 2 are:

\((\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2)\)
\((\mathbf{s}_2, \mathbf{s}_3)\)
\((\mathbf{s}_3, \mathbf{s}_4)\)
\((\mathbf{s}_4, \mathbf{s}_5)\)

We now calculate the squared differences for each pair of spatial points:
\[\begin{aligned}
\left( Z(\mathbf{s}_1) - Z(\mathbf{s}_2) \right)^2 &= (10 - 12)^2 = 4, \\
\left( Z(\mathbf{s}_2) - Z(\mathbf{s}_3) \right)^2 &= (12 - 14)^2 = 4, \\
\left( Z(\mathbf{s}_3) - Z(\mathbf{s}_4) \right)^2 &= (14 - 13)^2 = 1, \\
\left( Z(\mathbf{s}_4) - Z(\mathbf{s}_5) \right)^2 &= (13 - 15)^2 = 4.
\end{aligned}\]
Now, compute the empirical variogram:
\[\begin{equation*}
\hat{\gamma}(2) = \frac{1}{2 \times 4} \left( 4 + 4 + 1 + 4 \right) = \frac{1}{8} \times 13 = 1.625.
\end{equation*}\]
Thus, for \(\mathbf{h} = 2\) is \(\hat{\gamma}(2) = 1.625\).

title: Understanding Kriging (Part 1)
text:
4.2 Using the “gstat” package of R
The “gstat” package in R is a versatile tool used for geostatistical modelling, spatial prediction, and multivariable geostatistics (Pebesma 2004). It provides functionality for variogram modeling, Kriging, and conditional simulation, supporting univariate and multivariate spatial data. Some of the main features of this library are the following:

Computing the variogram \(\rightarrow\) empirical variogram (also called experimental) and variogram fitting (variogram modeling).
Kriging \(\rightarrow\) ordinary, simple, and universal kriging.
Multivariable geostatistics \(\rightarrow\) co-kriging and other methods for spatial modelling.
Simulation \(\rightarrow\) conditional and unconditional GRF for spatial predictions.

The “gstat” package is simple to use and here are the basics steps for spatial data analysis:

Define spatial data ( a \(\texttt{SpatialPointsDataFrame})\) from the “sp” package.
Compute the empirical variogram using the function \(\texttt{variogram()}\)
Fit a variogram model using the function \(\texttt{fit.variogram()}\)
Perform kriging prediction with the \(\texttt{krige()}\) function.

For the California air pollution data (from the “rspatial” package), select the “airqual” data and interpolate the levels of ozone (averages for 1980-2009). Here, you must consider “OZDLYAV” (unit is parts per billion) for interpolation purposes.

# Installing the rspat package
if (!require("rspatial")) remotes::install_github('rspatial/rspatial')

# Read the data
library(rspatial)
x <- sp_data("airqual")
x$res <- x$OZDLYAV * 1000

Now, we create a \(\texttt{SpatialPointsDataFrame}\) and transform to Teale Albers. Note the units=km, which was needed to fit the variogram.

#===================================
#         Installing rgdal
#===================================
# url <- "https://download.r-forge.r-project.org/bin/windows/contrib/4.4/rgdal_1.6-7.zip"
# install.packages(url, type="source", repos=NULL)

library(rgdal)
coordinates(x) <- ~LONGITUDE + LATITUDE
proj4string(x) <- CRS('+proj=longlat +datum=NAD83')
TA <- CRS("+proj=aea +lat_1=34 +lat_2=40.5 +lat_0=0 +lon_0=-120 +
          x_0=0 +y_0=-4000000 +datum=WGS84 +units=km")
coords <- spTransform(x, TA)

Now we will create an empirical variogram using the package “gstat” as follows:

library(gstat)
gs <- gstat(formula = res~1, locations = coords)
v <- variogram(gs, width=20)

title: Understanding Kriging (Part 1)
text:
5.1 Ordinary Kriging
Let consider the observed values \(\mathbf{Z} = (Z(\mathbf{s}_1), Z(\mathbf{s}_2), \dots, Z(\mathbf{s}_n))^{\top}\) at known locations \(\{\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2, \dots, \mathbf{s}_n\}\). The goal is to predict the value of a random field \(Z(\mathbf{s}_0)\) at an unobserved location \(\mathbf{s}_0\). The model assumption for this case is the following:
\[
\mathbf{Z} = \mu  + \delta(\mathbf{s}), \hspace{6mm} \mathbf{s} \in S, \hspace{2mm} \mu \in \mathbb{R} (\text{unknown})
\]
where \(\delta(\mathbf{s})\) is a zero-mean spatial stochastic process with variogram or with some covariance function and \(S \subset \mathbb{R}^{d}\), with \(d\) being a dimensional Euclidean space. For this case, Kriging assumes a spatial random field expressed through a variogram or covariance function, and allows to face this spatial rediction problem. In this case, the Ordinary Kriging predictor for \(Z(\mathbf{s}_0)\) is a linear combination of the observed values such that:
\[\begin{equation*}
\hat{Z}(\mathbf{s}_0) = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i Z(\mathbf{s}_i),
\end{equation*},\]
where \(w_i\), for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) are the Kriging weights that need to be calculated. In this way, Kriging minimizes the mean squared error of the prediction such that:
\[\begin{equation*}
\text{min} \hspace{2mm}\sigma^{2}_{\text{error}} = \mathbb{E}[Z(\mathbf{s}_0) - \hat{Z}(\mathbf{s}_0)]^{2}
\end{equation*},\]
or
\[
\text{min}\hspace{2mm} \sigma^{2}_{\text{error}} = \mathbb{E}[Z(\mathbf{s}_0) - \sum_{i=1}^n w_i Z(\mathbf{s}_i)]^{2}
\tag{5}\]
In terms of a covariance function, for a zero-mean and second order stationary spatial process, and also considering to \(C(\mathbf{h}), \mathbf{h} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\), then Equation 5 can be written as:
\[\begin{equation}
\sigma^{2}_{\text{error}} = C(0) - 2 \sum^{n}_{i=1}w_iC(\mathbf{s}_0, \mathbf{s}_i) + \sum^{n}_{i=1}\sum^{n}_{j=1} w_{i}w_{j}C(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{s}_j).
\end{equation}\]
The ordinary Kriging weights \(w_i\) must satisfy two requirements:

Unbiasedness: The predictor should be unbiased, which requires that \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i = 1\).
Optimality: The weights should minimize the variance of the prediction error (the Kriging variance), leading to the solution of a system of equations.

The unbiasedness requirement ensures that the expected value of the Kriging predictor matches the expected value of the random field, preventing systematic over- or under-prediction (interpolation).

title: Understanding Kriging (Part 1)
text:
5.2 Finding the Kriging weights
Based on the data \(\mathbf{Z}\) and \(\{\mathbf{s}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_n\}\), with \(C(\mathbf{h})\) being a covariance function of the spatial random field, and \(\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{s}_i - \mathbf{s}_j\), for Ordinary Kriging we can write a linear system of equations fo find the Kriging weights \(w_1, \ldots, w_n\). But, how can we propose this system of equations? Well, we already know that the ordinary Kriging estimator is a linear combination of the observed values,
\[\begin{equation*}
\hat{Z}(\mathbf{s}_0) = \sum^{n}_{i=1} w_i Z(\mathbf{s}_i),
\end{equation*}\]
and since that here we are considering the covariance then the minimization problem can be written as:
\[
\text{min} \hspace{2mm} C(0) - 2\sum^{n}_{i=1}w_{i}C(\mathbf{s}_0, \mathbf{s}_i) + \sum^{n}_{i=1}\sum^{n}_{j=1}w_{i}w_{j}C(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{s}_j) + 2\mathcal{M}(\sum^{n}_{i=1} w_i - 1)
\tag{6}\]
where \(\mathcal{M}\) is the Lagrange multiplier. Thus, after differentiating Equation 6 with respect \(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{n}\) and \(\mathcal{M}\), and set the derivatives equal to zero we have:
\[\begin{align*}
2\sum^{n}_{j=1}w_{j}C(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{s}_j) - 2C(\mathbf{s}_0, \mathbf{s}_i) - 2\mathcal{M} \hspace{2mm} = & 0 \\
\sum^{n}_{j=1}w_{j} C(\mathbf{s}_i - \mathbf{s}_j) + C(\mathbf{s}_0 - \mathbf{s}_i) - \mathcal{M} \hspace{2mm} = & \hspace{2mm} 0 \\
\sum^{n}_{i=1}w_{i} \hspace{2mm} = & \hspace{2mm} 1
\end{align*}\]
Therefore, using a matrix notation to find \(w_{1}, \ldots, w_{n}\) we propose the following linear system of equations:
\[
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{c},
\]
where:

\(\mathbf{w} = (w_{1}, \ldots, w_{n}, -\mathcal{M})^{\top}\).
\(\mathbf{c} = (C(\mathbf{s}_0, \mathbf{s}_1), \ldots, C(\mathbf{s}_0, \mathbf{s}_n), 1)^{\top}\).
\(\boldsymbol{\Gamma} = C(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{s}_j), \hspace{2mm} i = 1, \ldots, n, \hspace{2mm} j = 1, \ldots, n\).

Thus, expressed in a linear system of equations (the Kriging system):
\[\begin{equation*}
\begin{pmatrix}
C(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_1) & C(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2) & \dots & C(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_n) & 1 \\
C(\mathbf{s}_2, \mathbf{s}_1) & C(\mathbf{s}_2, \mathbf{s}_2) & \dots & C(\mathbf{s}_2, \mathbf{s}_n) & 1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
C(\mathbf{s}_n, \mathbf{s}_1) & C(\mathbf{s}_n, \mathbf{s}_2) & \dots & C(\mathbf{s}_n, \mathbf{s}_n) & 1 \\
1 & 1 & \dots & 1 & 0 \\
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
w_1 \\
w_2 \\
\vdots \\
w_n \\
-\mathcal{M} \\
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
C(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_0) \\
C(\mathbf{s}_2, \mathbf{s}_0) \\
\vdots \\
C(\mathbf{s}_n, \mathbf{s}_0) \\
1 \\
\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation*}\]
We can find \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}\) as
\[
\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{-1}\mathbf{c}.
\]
Finally, the Kriging variance, which quantifies the uncertainty of the prediction at \(\mathbf{s}_0\), is given by:
\[\begin{equation*}
\sigma_\text{OK}^2(\mathbf{s}_0) = C(\mathbf{0}) - \sum_{i=1}^n w_i C(\mathbf{s}_i - \mathbf{s}_0) - \mathcal{M}
\end{equation*},\]
where lower Kriging variance indicates a reliable prediction (interpolation) values.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
This tutorial explains and implements regTPS (Cavieres and Krumscheid, 2026 (in press)), a way of approximating a Gaussian random field (GRF) for Bayesian spatial models. The idea is to build the covariance of the field from a regularized thin plate spline (TPS) operator, expand it with a Karhunen-Loève expansion (KLE), and fit the resulting low-dimensional model by MCMC.
Let consider the geostatistical model
\[y_i = u(\mathbf{s}_i) + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2), \qquad i = 1, \dots, N,\]
where \(\mathbf{s}_i \in \mathcal{D} \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) and \(u(\cdot)\) is a GRF. No separate mean is included: the constant function belongs to the polynomial null space of the TPS penalty and is handled by the field itself.
The main steps to follow are:

Build a TPS basis and its penalty matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) (with mgcv).
Eigendecompose \(\mathbf{S}\) and order the eigenvalues \(v_k\) in ascending order.
Truncate the expansion at \(M\) modes using a variance-retention rule.
Place the prior \(z_k \sim \mathcal{N}\big(0, (1+\alpha v_k)^{-1}\big)\) on the coefficients, written in non-centered form.
Sample \((\tilde{\mathbf{z}}, \alpha, \sigma_\varepsilon)\) with HMC in Stan.

The sections below give the theory, then the code, then a simulation study.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
section: 2.1 Gaussian random fields and the Karhunen-Loève expansion
text:
2.1 Gaussian random fields and the Karhunen-Loève expansion
A GRF \(u(\mathbf{s})\) is a collection of random variables such that every finite subset is multivariate normal. It is fully specified by its mean and its covariance function \(C(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}')\). Covariance functions are symmetric and positive semidefinite, and under mild conditions they are Hilbert-Schmidt kernels. Mercer’s theorem then gives
\[C(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}') = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \lambda_k \, \phi_k(\mathbf{s})\, \phi_k(\mathbf{s}'),\]
where \((\lambda_k, \phi_k)\) solve the Fredholm eigenproblem
\[\int_{\mathcal{D}} C(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}')\, \phi_k(\mathbf{s}')\, d\mathbf{s}' = \lambda_k \phi_k(\mathbf{s}),
\qquad \langle \phi_k, \phi_\ell \rangle_{L^2} = \delta_{k\ell}.\]
Truncating at \(M\) terms gives the KLE of the field,
\[u(\mathbf{s}) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{M} \sqrt{\lambda_k}\, \phi_k(\mathbf{s})\, \epsilon_k, \qquad \epsilon_k \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1).\]
The practical difficulty is that the eigenpairs are known in closed form only for a few covariances. The regTPS-KLE construction avoids this by obtaining the eigensystem from a penalty matrix that is already available in standard spline software.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
section: 2.2 Thin plate splines and the bending energy
text:
2.2 Thin plate splines and the bending energy
For \(f \in H^2(\mathcal{D})\) the thin plate spline bending energy is
\[J(f) = \int_{\mathcal{D}} \left[ \left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial s_1^2}\right)^2 + 2\left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial s_1 \partial s_2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial s_2^2}\right)^2 \right] d\mathbf{s}.\]
Up to boundary terms this equals \(\int_{\mathcal{D}} (\Delta f)^2\, d\mathbf{s}\), and its Euler-Lagrange operator is the biharmonic operator \(\Delta^2\). \(J\) is a seminorm: \(J(f) = 0\) exactly when \(f\) is a polynomial of total degree at most 1, i.e. \(f \in \mathcal{P}_1 = \text{span}\{1, s_1, s_2\}\). This null space has dimension
\[d_{\text{null}} = \binom{d + m - 1}{d} = 3 \qquad (d = 2,\ m = 2).\]
A smoothing TPS minimizes the penalized least squares functional
\[\mathcal{L}(f) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \big(y_i - f(\mathbf{s}_i)\big)^2 + \alpha\, J(f), \qquad \alpha > 0.\]
The TPS kernel \(\eta(d) = d^2 \log d\) is the Green’s function of \(\Delta^2\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (up to the constant \(1/8\pi\)). It is only conditionally positive definite, so it is not a valid covariance function, and Mercer’s theorem and the KLE cannot be applied to it directly.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
2.3 Regularizing the operator
To obtain a proper covariance, regTPS-KLE replaces the singular biharmonic operator by the regularized elliptic operator
\[L_\alpha = \mathbf{I} + \alpha \Delta^2, \qquad \alpha > 0.\]
It arises from the continuous variational problem
\[\min_{f \in H^2(\mathcal{D})} \int_{\mathcal{D}} (f - g)^2\, d\mathbf{s} + \alpha J(f),\]
whose Euler-Lagrange equation is the fourth-order elliptic PDE \(L_\alpha f = g\). Under suitable boundary conditions \(L_\alpha\) is self-adjoint and boundedly invertible, and its inverse
\[(L_\alpha^{-1} g)(\mathbf{s}) = \int_{\mathcal{D}} K_\alpha(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}')\, g(\mathbf{s}')\, d\mathbf{s}'\]
is compact, self-adjoint and strictly positive definite. Its kernel \(K_\alpha\) is therefore a Hilbert-Schmidt kernel, and Mercer’s theorem applies:
\[K_\alpha(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}') = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \lambda_{k,\alpha}\, \phi_k(\mathbf{s})\, \phi_k(\mathbf{s}').\]

2.3.1 The spectrum of \(L_\alpha\)
Let \(v_k\) denote the eigenvalues of \(\Delta^2\) in ascending order, so \(\Delta^2 \phi_k = v_k \phi_k\). Because \(L_\alpha\) is a polynomial in \(\Delta^2\), it shares the eigenfunctions \(\phi_k\), and
\[L_\alpha \phi_k = (1 + \alpha v_k)\, \phi_k
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mu_k(\alpha) = 1 + \alpha v_k,
\qquad
\boxed{\;\lambda_{k,\alpha} = \frac{1}{1 + \alpha v_k}\;}\]
The spectrum has two regimes:

The parameter \(\alpha\) controls how fast \(\lambda_{k,\alpha}\) decays: larger \(\alpha\) shrinks rough modes harder and gives smoother, longer-range fields. It does not change the smoothness class of the field. The order of the operator does, and for \(\Delta^2\) in two dimensions the Matérn-type smoothness is \(\nu = \ell - d/2 = 2 - 1 = 1\).
Treating the null space explicitly, with unit variance, is a central feature of the method. The polynomial part is neither projected out nor penalized, so the field can represent large-scale trends.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
2.4 Finite-dimensional (Ritz-Galerkin) approximation
The eigenfunctions \(\phi_k\) are not available in closed form on a general domain. They are approximated in the space spanned by \(K\) TPS basis functions,
\[\mathcal{V}_K = \text{span}\{\tilde\phi_1, \dots, \tilde\phi_K\}, \qquad \tilde{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf{s}) = \big(\tilde\phi_1(\mathbf{s}), \dots, \tilde\phi_K(\mathbf{s})\big)^\top,\]
which in practice is the thin plate regression spline basis of mgcv (bs = "tp", k = K). In this basis, \(f(\mathbf{s}) = \tilde{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf{s})^\top \mathbf{c}\) and the bending energy becomes a quadratic form,
\[J(f) = \mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{S}\, \mathbf{c}, \qquad S_{jl} = \int_{\mathcal{D}} \Delta\tilde\phi_j(\mathbf{s})\, \Delta\tilde\phi_l(\mathbf{s})\, d\mathbf{s}.\]
The matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, with a null space of dimension \(d_{\text{null}}\). mgcv computes it in a numerically stable way without evaluating the integral. It is essential to build the basis without the sum-to-zero constraint (absorb.cons = FALSE), so that the constant and linear terms stay in the basis.

2.4.1 Eigendecomposition of the penalty
\[\mathbf{S} = \boldsymbol\Psi_S\, \mathbf{V}_S\, \boldsymbol\Psi_S^\top, \qquad
\mathbf{V}_S = \text{diag}(v_1 \le v_2 \le \dots \le v_K), \qquad
\boldsymbol\Psi_S^\top \boldsymbol\Psi_S = \mathbf{I}_K.\]
The first \(d_{\text{null}}\) eigenvalues are numerically zero and their eigenvectors span the polynomial trends. The \(k\)-th discrete eigenfunction is
\[\hat\phi_k(\mathbf{s}) = \tilde{\boldsymbol\phi}(\mathbf{s})^\top \boldsymbol\psi_{S,k}.\]
The eigenvalues \(v_k\) of \(\mathbf{S}\) approximate those of \(\Delta^2\) on \(\mathcal{V}_K\), and the approximation improves as \(K\) grows.
Standard versus generalized eigenproblem. A fully consistent Galerkin discretization solves the generalized problem \(\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol\psi = v\,\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol\psi\) with the \(L^2\) mass matrix \(M_{jk} = \int \tilde\phi_j\tilde\phi_k\, d\mathbf{s}\), which keeps the \(\hat\phi_k\) orthonormal in \(L^2\). regTPS-KLE instead solves the standard problem \(\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol\psi = v\boldsymbol\psi\), as is common in TPS software. Modes are then ranked purely by bending energy, and \(\alpha\) absorbs any constant scaling. This is a computational approximation (see Appendix A of the paper).

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
2.5 Discrete KLE with adaptive truncation
With the discrete eigenpairs, the covariance kernel is approximated by
\[K_\alpha(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}') \approx \sum_{k=1}^{M} \lambda_{k,\alpha}\, \hat\phi_k(\mathbf{s})\, \hat\phi_k(\mathbf{s}'), \qquad \lambda_{k,\alpha} = \frac{1}{1 + \alpha v_k}.\]
The truncation level \(M \le K\) is chosen to retain a proportion \(\gamma\) (typically 0.95 to 0.99) of the total KLE variance:
\[M = \min\left\{ m : \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{m} \lambda_{k,\alpha}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{k,\alpha}} \ge \gamma \right\}.\]
Because the truncation is decided before sampling, it needs a fixed reference value of \(\alpha\). The implementation below uses
\[\alpha_{\text{ref,scaled}} = \frac{\alpha_{\text{ref}}}{\text{median}\{v_k : v_k > 10^{-10}\}},\]
which makes the truncation rule independent of the numerical scale of \(\mathbf{S}\). It also forces \(\lambda_k = 1\) for \(k \le d_{\text{null}}\) and requires \(M \ge d_{\text{null}} + 5\), so that a few penalized modes are always kept. This \(\alpha_{\text{ref,scaled}}\) is used only to choose \(M\) and to initialize the sampler. The \(\alpha\) that enters the prior is estimated.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
2.6 Bayesian formulation

2.6.1 Prior on the coefficients
Writing \(f = \tilde{\boldsymbol\phi}^\top\mathbf{c}\), the penalty \(J(f) = \mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{S}\mathbf{c}\) corresponds to a Gaussian prior on \(\mathbf{c}\) with precision matrix
\[\mathbf{P}_\alpha = \mathbf{I} + \alpha\mathbf{S}, \qquad \mathbf{c} \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{P}_\alpha^{-1}\big).\]
In the rotated coordinates \(\mathbf{z} = \boldsymbol\Psi_S^\top \mathbf{c}\), the precision becomes diagonal, \(\mathbf{I} + \alpha\mathbf{V}_S\), so the components are independent:
\[z_k \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \lambda_{k,\alpha}\right), \qquad \lambda_{k,\alpha} = \frac{1}{1 + \alpha v_k}.\]
The field is then \(f(\mathbf{s}) = \sum_{k=1}^{M} z_k \hat\phi_k(\mathbf{s}) = \boldsymbol\Phi(\mathbf{s})^\top\mathbf{z}\).


2.6.2 Non-centered parameterization
To decouple the latent coefficients from the hyperparameter \(\alpha\) and improve HMC geometry, we sample standard normal variables \(\tilde z_k\) and set
\[z_k = \sqrt{\lambda_{k,\alpha}}\,\tilde z_k =
\begin{cases}
\tilde z_k, & k \le d_{\text{null}},\\[4pt]
\dfrac{\tilde z_k}{\sqrt{1 + \alpha v_k}}, & k > d_{\text{null}},
\end{cases}
\qquad \tilde z_k \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1).\]


2.6.3 Likelihood and priors
Let \(\boldsymbol\Psi_M \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times M}\) contain the first \(M\) eigenvectors and \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\Phi} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times K}\) the TPS basis at the observed sites. The KLE design matrices are
\[\boldsymbol\Phi_{\text{obs}} = \tilde{\boldsymbol\Phi}\,\boldsymbol\Psi_M \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times M},
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Phi_{\text{grid}} = \tilde{\boldsymbol\Phi}_{\text{grid}}\,\boldsymbol\Psi_M,\]
and the likelihood is
\[\mathbf{y} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{z}}, \alpha, \sigma_\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\boldsymbol\Phi_{\text{obs}}\,\mathbf{z}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}, \alpha),\ \sigma_\varepsilon^2 \mathbf{I}_N\big).\]
The hyperpriors are
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma_\varepsilon &\sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda_\sigma), \qquad \lambda_\sigma = -\frac{\log p_\sigma}{\sigma_0}, \quad \Pr(\sigma_\varepsilon > \sigma_0) = p_\sigma,\\
\log\alpha &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\alpha^2),\\
\tilde z_k &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad k = 1,\dots,M.
\end{aligned}\]
The exponential prior on \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) is a penalized complexity (PC) prior. We use \(\sigma_0 = 0.5\) and \(p_\sigma = 0.05\). The joint posterior is
\[p(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}, \alpha, \sigma_\varepsilon \mid \mathbf{y}) \propto
\left[\prod_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{N}\big(y_i \mid (\boldsymbol\Phi_{\text{obs}}\mathbf{z})_i, \sigma_\varepsilon^2\big)\right]
\prod_{k=1}^{M}\mathcal{N}(\tilde z_k \mid 0, 1)\ \pi(\alpha)\ \pi(\sigma_\varepsilon).\]


2.6.4 Prediction
For any set of new locations, the field is \(\boldsymbol\Phi_{\text{new}}\mathbf{z}\) with \(\boldsymbol\Phi_{\text{new}} = \tilde{\boldsymbol\Phi}_{\text{new}}\boldsymbol\Psi_M\). Each posterior draw of \(\mathbf{z}\) gives one draw of the field, so uncertainty in \(\alpha\), \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) and the coefficients propagates automatically.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
3.1 The regTPS function
regTPS_s() performs steps 1 to 3. It contains no inference code and returns everything needed by the Stan model.

regTPS_s <- function(sp_points, grid_total, y_obs, k_basis,
                     variance_threshold = 0.95, alpha_ref = 1,
                     verbose = TRUE) {

  #====================================
  # Basis and penalty (no centering constraint, so the null space is kept)
  #====================================
  data_smooth <- data.frame(s1 = sp_points$s1, s2 = sp_points$s2, y_obs = y_obs)
  sm <- mgcv::smoothCon(s(s1, s2, k = k_basis, bs = "tp"),
                        data = data_smooth, absorb.cons = FALSE)[[1]]

  Phi_basis_sp   <- PredictMat(sm, data_smooth)
  Phi_basis_grid <- PredictMat(sm, grid_total)
  S <- sm$S[[1]]

  #====================================
  # Eigendecomposition (S psi = v psi), cleaned and ordered ascending
  #====================================
  S_eig    <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE)
  S_diag   <- S_eig$values
  evectors <- S_eig$vectors

  S_diag[abs(S_diag) < 1e-12] <- 0
  if (any(S_diag < -1e-10))
    warning("Negative eigenvalues detected (max magnitude: ",
            max(abs(S_diag[S_diag < 0])), ")")
  S_diag[S_diag < 0] <- 0

  order_idx <- order(S_diag, decreasing = FALSE)
  S_diag    <- S_diag[order_idx]
  evectors  <- evectors[, order_idx]

  M_P_null_space <- sm$null.space.dim

  #====================================
  # Variance-based truncation
  #====================================
  nonzero_eigs <- S_diag[S_diag > 1e-10]
  if (length(nonzero_eigs) == 0) stop("No non-zero eigenvalues found.")

  # reference alpha, rescaled so that the rule does not depend on the scale of S
  alpha_ref_scaled <- alpha_ref / median(nonzero_eigs)
  lambda_k <- 1 / (1 + alpha_ref_scaled * S_diag)
  lambda_k[1:M_P_null_space] <- 1            # null space: unit variance

  total_variance <- sum(lambda_k)
  cumvar <- cumsum(lambda_k) / total_variance

  M_truncation <- which(cumvar >= variance_threshold)[1]
  if (is.na(M_truncation)) M_truncation <- length(S_diag)

  M_truncation <- max(M_truncation, M_P_null_space + 5)
  if (M_truncation < M_P_null_space) M_truncation <- M_P_null_space

  var_explained <- sum(lambda_k[1:M_truncation]) / total_variance

  if (verbose) {
    cat("Null space dim:", M_P_null_space, "| basis:", length(S_diag),
        "| non-zero eig:", sum(S_diag > 1e-10), "\n")
    cat("alpha_ref scaled:", round(alpha_ref_scaled, 6),
        "| M_truncation:", M_truncation,
        "| variance explained:", round(100 * var_explained, 2), "%\n")
  }

  #====================================
  # Truncated matrices
  #====================================
  idx <- 1:M_truncation
  Phi_kle_sp       <- Phi_basis_sp   %*% evectors[, idx]
  Phi_kle_grid     <- Phi_basis_grid %*% evectors[, idx]
  S_diag_truncated <- S_diag[idx]

  list(Phi_kle_sp         = Phi_kle_sp,
       Phi_kle_grid       = Phi_kle_grid,
       S_diag_truncated   = S_diag_truncated,
       M_truncation       = M_truncation,
       M_P_null_space     = M_P_null_space,
       alpha_ref_scaled   = alpha_ref_scaled,
       variance_explained = var_explained,
       k_basis            = k_basis,
       S_diag_full        = S_diag,
       lambda_k           = lambda_k,
       cumvar             = cumvar,
       evectors           = evectors,
       sm                 = sm)
}

The objects nedded to use regTPS_s() are:

sp_points, grid_total: data frames with columns s1 and s2, for the observed sites and the prediction locations. The column names must be exactly these because they appear in the mgcv formula.
y_obs: the response variable, used only to build the smoothing data frame.
k_basis: the number of TPS basis functions \(K\). It must be smaller than the number of distinct sites.
variance_threshold: the proportion \(\gamma\) of KLE variance to retain.
alpha_ref: the reference \(\alpha\) used for the truncation rule.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
section: 5.1 Simulate a Matérn field with Gaussian noise
text:
5.1 Simulate a Matérn field with Gaussian noise
We simulate a Matérn (\(\nu = 3/2\)) field jointly at 200 random observed sites and a \(30\times 30\) prediction grid, then add Gaussian noise at the observed sites. The fitted model uses a TPS prior, so it is not the true data-generating covariance; this is the usual stress test for the approximation.

set.seed(123)

# Settings
n_obs       <- 200     # number of observed locations
n_grid_pred <- 30      # prediction grid is n_grid_pred x n_grid_pred
sigma_e     <- 0.5     # true noise sd
sigma_u     <- 1.0     # true marginal sd of the field
range_u     <- 0.3     # spatial range (domain is [0,1]^2)
mu0         <- 0       # constant mean

# Locations
sp_points  <- data.frame(s1 = runif(n_obs), s2 = runif(n_obs))
g          <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n_grid_pred)
grid_total <- expand.grid(s1 = g, s2 = g)

all_pts <- rbind(sp_points, grid_total)
n_sp    <- nrow(sp_points)
n_grid  <- nrow(grid_total)

# True covariance (Matern, nu = 3/2)
matern32 <- function(d, sigma, rho) {
  h <- sqrt(3) * d / rho
  sigma^2 * (1 + h) * exp(-h)
}
D        <- as.matrix(dist(all_pts))
Cov_true <- matern32(D, sigma_u, range_u)

# Simulate the field at observed and grid locations jointly
L     <- chol(Cov_true + diag(1e-8, nrow(Cov_true)))   # upper triangular
u_all <- mu0 + as.vector(t(L) %*% rnorm(nrow(Cov_true)))

u_true_sp   <- u_all[1:n_sp]
u_true_grid <- u_all[(n_sp + 1):(n_sp + n_grid)]

# Gaussian observation noise
y_obs <- u_true_sp + rnorm(n_sp, mean = 0, sd = sigma_e)


image(g, g, matrix(u_true_grid, n_grid_pred, n_grid_pred),
      xlab = "s1", ylab = "s2", main = "True field and observed locations")
points(sp_points$s1, sp_points$s2, pch = 19, cex = 0.5)

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
5.2 Build the regTPS basis
We use \(K = 150\) basis functions and keep 95% of the KLE variance.

variance_threshold <- 0.95

reg <- regTPS_s(sp_points, grid_total, y_obs, k_basis = 150,
                variance_threshold = variance_threshold, alpha_ref = 1)

Null space dim: 3 | basis: 150 | non-zero eig: 147 
alpha_ref scaled: 0.000408 | M_truncation: 123 | variance explained: 95.07 %



5.2.1 Inspecting the spectrum and the truncation
The penalty eigenvalues are zero for the first \(d_{\text{null}} = 3\) modes and then grow quickly. The KLE variances \(\lambda_k\) therefore decay, and the cumulative variance saturates well before \(K\) modes.

M  <- reg$M_truncation
M0 <- reg$M_P_null_space
K  <- length(reg$S_diag_full)

df_spec <- data.frame(k = 1:K, v = reg$S_diag_full,
                      type = ifelse(1:K <= M0, "Null space", "Penalized"))

p_spec <- ggplot(df_spec, aes(k, pmax(v, 1e-6), colour = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = M, linetype = 2) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Penalty eigenvalues", x = "Mode index (increasing roughness)",
       y = expression(v[k]~"(null modes floored at 1e-6)"), colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

df_cum <- data.frame(k = 1:K, cumvar = reg$cumvar)

p_cum <- ggplot(df_cum, aes(k, cumvar)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = variance_threshold, linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = M, linetype = 2) +
  labs(title = paste0("Cumulative variance (M = ", M, ")"),
       x = "Number of basis functions", y = "Cumulative proportion") +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(p_spec, p_cum, ncol = 2)

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
6.1 Data, priors and initial values
The PC prior for \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) states \(\Pr(\sigma_\varepsilon > 0.5) = 0.05\). For \(\log\alpha\) we use \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\alpha^2)\). The paper reports \(\sigma_\alpha = 3\), while the TMB and Stan code used so far in this project fixed it at 1, so it is exposed as a data input (see the notes at the end).

sigma_prior_s0    <- 0.5     # P(sigma > 0.5) = 0.05
sigma_prior_alpha <- 0.05
lambda_sigma_e    <- -log(sigma_prior_alpha) / sigma_prior_s0
sigma_logalpha    <- 1.0       

stan_dat <- list(N                = length(y_obs),
                 N_grid           = nrow(reg$Phi_kle_grid),
                 M                = reg$M_truncation,
                 M0               = reg$M_P_null_space,
                 y_obs            = as.vector(y_obs),
                 Phi_kle_sp       = unname(as.matrix(reg$Phi_kle_sp)),
                 Phi_kle_grid     = unname(as.matrix(reg$Phi_kle_grid)),
                 S_diag_truncated = as.vector(reg$S_diag_truncated),
                 lambda_sigma_e   = lambda_sigma_e,
                 sigma_logalpha   = sigma_logalpha)

logalpha_init <- max(min(log(reg$alpha_ref_scaled), 3), -3)
sigma_init    <- sd(y_obs)

stan_init <- function(chain_id) {
  list(z_tilde  = as.array(rep(0, reg$M_truncation)),
       logalpha = logalpha_init,
       sigma_e  = sigma_init)
}

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
6.2 Sampling
The fit is cached in an .rds file so that re-knitting does not resample. Delete regTPS_fit.rds after changing the data, the basis or the Stan program.

fit_file <- "regTPS_fit.rds"

if (file.exists(fit_file)) {
  stan_fit <- readRDS(fit_file)
} else {
  stan_fit <- sampling(regTPS_mod,
                       data    = stan_dat,
                       init    = stan_init,
                       chains  = 4,
                       iter    = 2000,
                       warmup  = 1000,
                       seed    = 123,
                       control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9),
                       refresh = 0)
  saveRDS(stan_fit, fit_file)
}

The true noise standard deviation is 0.5. The posterior of \(\log\alpha\) can be compared with its prior to see how much the data inform the smoothing:

post <- rstan::extract(stan_fit)

ggplot(data.frame(logalpha = post$logalpha), aes(logalpha)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = sigma_logalpha),
                colour = "red") +
  labs(title = expression("Posterior (blue) and prior (red) of"~log~alpha),
       x = expression(log~alpha), y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
section: 6.4 How the prior and the data interact mode by mode
text:
6.4 How the prior and the data interact mode by mode
For each retained mode we compare the posterior mean of \(|z_k|\) with the prior standard deviation \(\sqrt{\lambda_{k,\alpha}}\) (averaged over the posterior of \(\alpha\)). Under a prior-dominated mode, \(\mathbb{E}|z_k| = \sqrt{2/\pi}\,\text{SD}_{\text{prior}}(z_k)\), which is the dashed line. Points above the line indicate that the data push the coefficient to larger values than the prior alone would; points near or below it indicate little data-driven learning. The null-space modes (unit prior SD) separate clearly from the penalized ones.

df_z <- data.frame(prior_sd = colMeans(post$scale),
                   abs_z    = abs(colMeans(post$z)),
                   type     = ifelse(1:M <= M0, "Null space", "Penalized"))

ggplot(df_z, aes(prior_sd, abs_z, colour = type, shape = type)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = log10(sqrt(2 / pi)), linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = expression("Prior SD"~sqrt(lambda[k])),
       y = expression("|Posterior mean of"~z[k]~"|"),
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
7.1 Posterior summaries on the grid

spat_field <- post$field_grid        # draws x N_grid

post_mean <- colMeans(spat_field)
post_sd   <- apply(spat_field, 2, sd)
post_lo   <- apply(spat_field, 2, quantile, 0.025)
post_hi   <- apply(spat_field, 2, quantile, 0.975)

df <- data.frame(s1 = grid_total$s1, s2 = grid_total$s2,
                 truth = u_true_grid, post_mean = post_mean, post_sd = post_sd,
                 err = post_mean - u_true_grid,
                 inside = u_true_grid >= post_lo & u_true_grid <= post_hi)

rmse     <- sqrt(mean(df$err^2))
mae      <- mean(abs(df$err))
r2       <- 1 - sum(df$err^2) / sum((df$truth - mean(df$truth))^2)
corr     <- cor(df$truth, df$post_mean)
coverage <- mean(df$inside)

data.frame(RMSE = rmse, MAE = mae, R2 = r2, Correlation = corr,
           Coverage95 = coverage)

       RMSE      MAE        R2 Correlation Coverage95
1 0.1957667 0.150504 0.9485536   0.9742802       0.91


Here \(R^2 = 1 - \sum_i (\hat u_i - u_i)^2 / \sum_i (u_i - \bar u)^2\) and Coverage95 is the proportion of grid points whose true value lies inside the 95% credible interval.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
7.2 Maps

lims       <- range(c(df$truth, df$post_mean))
fld_scale  <- scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = lims, option = "D")
base_theme <- theme_minimal() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

p_true <- ggplot(df, aes(s1, s2, fill = truth)) +
  geom_raster() + fld_scale + coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "True GRF", fill = "u") + base_theme

p_est <- ggplot(df, aes(s1, s2, fill = post_mean)) +
  geom_raster() + fld_scale + coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Posterior mean", fill = "u") + base_theme

p_err <- ggplot(df, aes(s1, s2, fill = err)) +
  geom_raster() + coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Error (posterior mean - truth)", fill = "err") + base_theme

p_sd <- ggplot(df, aes(s1, s2, fill = post_sd)) +
  geom_raster() + coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma") +
  labs(title = "Posterior SD", fill = "sd") + base_theme

p_scatter <- ggplot(df, aes(truth, post_mean)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "red") +
  labs(title = sprintf("Truth vs estimate (RMSE = %.3f)", rmse),
       x = "True field", y = "Posterior mean") +
  theme_minimal()

p_cover <- ggplot(df, aes(s1, s2, fill = inside)) +
  geom_raster() + coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "grey85", "FALSE" = "red"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "inside", "FALSE" = "outside")) +
  labs(title = sprintf("95%% CI coverage: %.1f%%", 100 * coverage),
       fill = "truth") + base_theme

grid.arrange(p_true, p_est, p_err, p_sd, p_scatter, p_cover, ncol = 3)








Panels to look at first: the posterior SD should be smallest near observed sites and larger in gaps, and the error map should show no obvious spatial pattern. Because the data come from a Matérn field and the model has a fixed TPS smoothness (\(\nu = 1\)), some systematic mismatch is expected.

title: regTPS - Approximating a GRF for Bayesian Spatial Modelling
text:
7.3 Posterior predictive check
Each posterior draw produces a replicated data set y_sim. The thin lines are the densities of 100 replicates and the thick line is the observed data.

y_sim <- post$y_sim
idx   <- sample(nrow(y_sim), 100)

dens_obs <- density(y_obs)
dens_rep <- lapply(idx, function(i) density(y_sim[i, ]))
ymax     <- max(dens_obs$y, sapply(dens_rep, function(d) max(d$y)))
xr       <- range(dens_obs$x, sapply(dens_rep, function(d) range(d$x)))

plot(dens_obs, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, ymax), xlim = xr,
     main = "Posterior predictive check", xlab = "y")
for (d in dens_rep) lines(d, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.25))
lines(dens_obs, lwd = 2)
